Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from all the gathered material.

---

# Malachi 2 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

Malachi 2 falls into two main sections: **vv. 1–9** (the rebuke of the unfaithful priests, contrasted with the ideal of Levi) and **vv. 10–17** (the rebuke of the people for mixed marriages, divorce, and wearying God with cynical words). The chapter is built around God's covenant — the covenant with Levi (vv. 4–8) and the marriage covenant (vv. 14–16). (EnduringWord.com, PreceptAustin.org)

---

## v. 1 — "And now this decree is for you, O priests"

- **"Commandment" = decree.** Ellicott notes the Hebrew term is better translated "decree" (as in Nahum 1:14; Psalm 7:6), since no explicit commandment is given — only a threat of punishment. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary** agrees: the threat is called a "commandment" because God ordains it and imposes its execution on certain instruments (cf. Leviticus 25:21). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/malachi/2.htm)
- **Precept Austin** (citing NICOT) notes the introductory "And now" (weattâ) recapitulates the preceding rebuke and emphasizes the new topic. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/malachi_2_commentary)
- **Guzik / EnduringWord**: The decree is aimed directly at the priests who had descended into hollow formalism. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)

---

## v. 2 — "If you do not listen … I will send a curse among you, and I will curse your blessings"

- **Two failures identified.** Guzik notes two priestly failures: (1) failure to listen to God, and (2) failure to have a heart burden for the glory of God. Their sin was a religion of surface emotions and outward signs, not of the heart. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)
- **Piper (DesiringGod)**, in a sermon on this passage, identifies the same two failures: failure to listen and failure to set the heart to honour God's name. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-curse-of-priestly-failure)
- **"Curse your blessings" — two interpretations.** Ellicott notes some take "your blessings" as the priests' tithes and portions of sacrifices (using "blessing" to mean "gift," cf. Genesis 33:11); others take it as the priestly benediction pronounced on the people (Numbers 6:23–27), which God would turn into curses. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary** favours the benediction view: God would not ratify the blessings the priests pronounced but would turn them into curses, also punishing the people who connived at the priests' iniquities. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/malachi/2.htm)
- **Precept Austin** calls this a "divine oxymoron — cursed blessings!" and notes the curse language is an almost exact quotation of Deuteronomy 28:20: the curse is "the inevitable counterpart of the covenant blessing." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/malachi_2_commentary)
- **"I have already begun to curse them."** The curse had already started to work. Pulpit notes a possible allusion to Nehemiah 13:1–2 where God turned Balaam's intended curse into a blessing — now the reverse would happen. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/malachi/2.htm)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** adds that even physical prosperity would be taken away, as forewarned in Deuteronomy 27–28. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/malachi-2.html)

---

## v. 3 — "I will rebuke your descendants … spread dung on your faces … you will be carried off with it"

- **"Rebuke your descendants" — textual issue.** The KJV reads "corrupt your seed," which some take as rotting crops, others as posterity. Ellicott favours "I will destroy for you the seed — viz., of the crops," noting that because the people neglected tithes, the Levites had to till fields (Nehemiah 13:10). LXX reads "corn." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **Precept Austin**, however, favours the "posterity/descendants" view citing the example of Eli and his sons (1 Samuel 2:27–33). The NET renders it "discipline your children." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/malachi_2_commentary)
- **"Spread dung on your faces" — graphic shaming.** Per the Law, the dung of sacrificial animals was to be carried outside the camp and burned (Exodus 29:14). Guzik says God would "rub their noses in it." The priests who profaned God's name by offering unfit animals would be treated with the utmost ignominy. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary** adds: the dung was actually the perquisite of the priests (the maw, Deuteronomy 18:3), which gives a "peculiar point" to the threat — "you shall get the dung of the maw as your perquisite instead of the maw." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/malachi/2.htm)
- **MacArthur** (cited at Precept Austin): the priests would "suffer humiliation and loss of office." Wiersbe: "You're treating Me with disrespect, so I'll treat you like garbage!" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/malachi_2_commentary)
- **"You will be carried off with it"** — they would be treated like the dung: removed from the sanctuary, disqualified, rejected. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/malachi_2_commentary)

---

## v. 4 — "Then you will know that I have sent you this commandment so that My covenant with Levi may continue"

- **Purpose of the discipline.** Guzik notes God's motive is redemptive: the Lord hoped this warning would make the priests properly respect His covenant. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)
- **Ellicott** offers a more severe reading: the new "decree" replaces the old covenant — "so that this new decree … may be my covenant with him instead of the old one." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary** finds Ellicott's reading "too involved and refined" and prefers "Because my covenant was with Levi" — God warned the priests because He willed the covenant with Levi to hold good, and He wanted priests who would maintain the true priestly character. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/malachi/2.htm)
- **TGC (Reformed)** explains "My covenant with Levi" as referring poetically to the responsibilities God entrusted to the tribe of Levi and the priests descending from Aaron. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/malachi/)

---

## v. 5 — "My covenant with him was one of life and peace … it called for reverence, and he revered Me"

- **Two sides of the covenant.** God gave "life and peace"; Levi rendered "fear" (reverence). Ellicott: "life in its highest sense; peace as the sum total of blessing." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary** explains the pronominal suffix issue: many Hebrew manuscripts lack "them," reading simply "I gave him fear. So the Vulgate: *Dedi eis timorem et timuit me* ("I gave them fear and he feared me"). This expresses man's part in the covenant: God gave blessings on condition that Levi feared, reverenced, worshipped, and obeyed the Lord. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/malachi/2.htm)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: the covenant was one of an "everlasting priesthood," and "the keeping of the law of the Lord is (exists as) life and peace; for obedience to it has its own rewards" (Psalm 19:11). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/malachi-2.html)
- **TGC (Reformed)** notes this is "a covenant of fear" — the profound awe, respect, and reverence for the Creator God as more holy, wise, and powerful than we can conceive. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/malachi/)

---

## v. 6 — "True instruction was in his mouth … nothing false … He walked with Me in peace and uprightness, and he turned many from iniquity"

- **The ideal priest described.** Guzik lists four marks: reverence, knowing God's word, godly character, and preserving/promoting God's word. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)
- **Ellicott**: "The law of truth" means right instruction in the Law and judgment in accordance with the Law. "Walked with me" alludes to Enoch (Genesis 5:24) — having their "conversation in heaven" (Philippians 3:20). Ellicott quotes Pusey: "What a history of zeal for the glory of God and of the conversion of sinners in those of whom the world knows nothing." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: "Not only his teaching was true, but his life was pure and good; he was the friend of God, living as always in his presence." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/malachi/2.htm)
- **Precept Austin**: The NET version reads "He taught what was true; sinful words were not found on his lips." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/malachi_2_commentary)

---

## v. 7 — "For the lips of a priest should preserve knowledge … he is the messenger of the LORD of Hosts"

- **The priest as teacher.** This was the priest's primary duty: to study the Law and teach it faithfully. Ellicott: "'Keep' — not as in a repository, but rather observe — i.e., speak in accordance with the knowledge of God, as revealed in the Law." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **Pulpit**: The priest was the appointed interpreter of the Law (Leviticus 10:11; Deuteronomy 17:9–11; 33:10). He "announces God's will to men, explaining the Law to meet the varied circumstances which occur in daily life." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/malachi/2.htm)
- **"Messenger of the LORD"** — literally "angel." Precept Austin notes this is a rare description (used of Haggai in Haggai 1:13 and of Christ Himself in Malachi 3:1). TGC adds this phrase is "normally reserved for the angel of the Lord, who speaks directly for God." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/malachi_2_commentary; https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/malachi/)
- **Guzik**: Leaders should be knowledgeable messengers of God's word. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)

---

## v. 8 — "But you have departed from the way … your instruction has caused many to stumble. You have violated the covenant of Levi"

- **The real vs. the ideal.** The priests did the exact reverse of what Levi exemplified. Ellicott: "ye have given them false instruction in the Law, and allowed those things which were forbidden … ye have turned the Law, which ought to have been a light … into a stumbling-block." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **Guzik**: Instead of keeping God's word with knowledge, reverence, and obedience, they "departed from the way" and "caused many to stumble at the law." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)
- **TGC**: The priests' humiliation resulted from failure in their duties — especially the task of instruction (teaching God's Word to God's people, Deuteronomy 33:10). (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/malachi/)
- **Piper (DesiringGod)** lists five failures from vv. 2, 8, 9: failure to listen, failure to honour God's name, departing from the way, causing many to stumble, and showing partiality. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-curse-of-priestly-failure)

---

## v. 9 — "So I in turn have made you despised and humiliated before all the people, because you have … shown partiality in matters of the law"

- **God's reciprocal judgment.** Because the priests failed to honour God, God caused them to be dishonoured before the people. Ellicott: "I am no longer bound by the covenant I made with the tribe of Levi, and, instead of 'life and peace,' I give you contempt." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **"Partiality in the law"** — the priests perverted judgment, showing favouritism in the administration of justice. Pulpit names this as "the most flagrant" sin of the priests (cf. Micah 3:11). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/malachi/2.htm)
- **Dr. Constable (Evangelical)** notes the priests "had become political pawns of the influential in Israel who used religion to maintain respectability." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/malachi-2.html)

---

## v. 10 — "Do we not all have one Father? Did not one God create us? Why then do we break faith with one another?"

- **"One Father" — not universal fatherhood.** Guzik explicitly states: "This does not teach the idea of the universal fatherhood of God, the doctrine that all are inherently right with God, or that God is everyone's father in the same way. This is a simple assertion that because we are all made in the image of God, we must respect and deal honorably with all." He adds it may also refer to their common Father in Abraham. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)
- **Ellicott** disagrees: the "one father" is God Himself (Malachi 1:6; Deuteronomy 32:6, 18), who is the spiritual Father of the nation. He explicitly rejects Adam, Abraham, or Jacob as the referent. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary** also identifies the Father as Almighty God (citing Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 63:16) and notes that the parallelism with "one God created us" supports this. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/malachi/2.htm)
- **Piper (DesiringGod)**: The verse addresses "widespread dishonesty … people were not keeping their word. Trusts were being broken." The treachery is first stated generally before Malachi zeroes in on marriage. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/let-none-be-faithless-to-the-wife-of-his-youth)
- **TGC**: This provides the theological basis for why marital faithlessness is wrong — all Israelites share one Father and Creator, making treachery against a fellow Israelite (especially a spouse) a profanation of the covenant. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/malachi/)

> **Protestant differences on v. 10:** The key question is whether "one Father" teaches universal spiritual fatherhood (all humans are children of God) or covenant fatherhood (God as Father of Israel specifically, or of all in a creational sense only). Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic) explicitly denies universal fatherhood; Ellicott and Pulpit (older Anglican) see it as God as Father of the covenant nation. The TGC (Reformed) sees it as creational and covenantal, providing the ground for why faithlessness within the covenant community is sin.

---

## v. 11 — "Judah has broken faith … marrying the daughter of a foreign god"

- **The sin is religious, not racial.** Guzik emphasises: "God's command against mixed marriages in Israel had nothing to do with race, but with faith." Ruth the Moabitess is an example of a foreign wife who forsook her gods for the LORD and was accepted (and is in Jesus' genealogy). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)
- **"Daughter of a foreign god"** — a woman who worships a strange god (Ellicott). Such marriages were forbidden in Exodus 34:16 and Deuteronomy 7:3. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **"Profaned the LORD's beloved sanctuary"** — Pulpit notes two main views: (1) the temple itself was profaned by heathen wives entering it, or (2) "the sanctuary" means the chosen nation itself, the community beloved by God which was holy by election (Exodus 19:6; Ezra 9:2; Nehemiah 13:29). Pulpit favours the latter. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/malachi/2.htm)
- **TGC (Reformed)** explains: "The Lord opposes marriage to 'the daughter of a foreign god,' not the daughter of foreign parents … A bride (or bridegroom) who remains devoted to a rival deity cannot unite fully with a spouse who belongs to the God of Israel." (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/malachi/)
- **Guzik** adds that marriage is described as "the LORD's holy institution which He loves" — it is holy to God, an institution He established, and something He loves. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)

---

## v. 12 — "May the LORD cut off … everyone who is awake and aware—even if he brings an offering"

- **"Awake and aware" — a difficult phrase.** Ellicott notes the Hebrew expression occurs only here. The Talmudic interpretation is "master and scholar," but Ellicott finds this "unsuitable." He prefers Gesenius's view: "watchman and answerer" — a military phrase for the sentinel's challenge and response, meaning "all living persons" / "all posterity." The Targum renders it "son and son's son." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **Pulpit** similarly notes it is "a kind of alliterative proverbial saying to express totality, everybody," though its exact origin is uncertain. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/malachi/2.htm)
- **Guzik** notes various translations: "master and scholar," "tempter and tempted," "witness and advocate," "kith and kin," or "nomads and settlers" — "Obviously, the Hebrew idiom is just another way of saying 'everyone'" (Alden). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: The phrase means "whether they were master or scholar, teacher or pupil, priest or one of the common people." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/malachi-2.html)

---

## v. 13 — "You cover the altar of the LORD with tears … He no longer regards your offerings"

- **The tears are those of the abandoned wives.** Guzik, citing Keil: "They cover the altar of Jehovah with tears, namely, by compelling the wives who have been put away to lay their trouble before God in the sanctuary." The priests' own neglected wives came and wept at the altar; when the husbands then offered sacrifice, it offended God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)
- **Pulpit**: "A multitude of repudiated wives coming to the temple with weeping and lamentation, and laying their cause before the Lord. This cruel and wicked conduct raised a barrier between them and God." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/malachi/2.htm)
- **Guzik** applies this to modern ministers: "It is a disgrace if a pastor or preacher's harsh, neglectful, or unkind treatment of his wife causes her to cry out before God." Trapp is quoted: "You caused your poor wives, when they should have been cheerful in God's service … to cover the Lord's altar with tears." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)

---

## v. 14 — "The LORD has been a witness between you and the wife of your youth … your companion and your wife by covenant"

- **God as witness to the marriage covenant.** Ellicott compares Genesis 31:49–50: "The LORD watch between me and thee … If thou shalt afflict my daughters … no man is with us; see, God is witness betwixt me and thee." He adds the wry note: "If people would seriously consider the meaning of this verse of Genesis, they would not be so fond of putting MIZPAH on their rings, for it denotes a strong suspicion as to the fidelity of the other party." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **Guzik**: The priests sinned by forsaking the wife they married in their youth, by breaking the goal of marriage (she is your *companion*) and by breaking the bond of marriage (*your wife by covenant*). Adam Clarke noted: "They kept their wives till they had passed their youth, and then put them away, that they might get young ones in their place." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)
- **Pulpit**: "The wife of thy youth" — whom you married when your affections were pure and fresh (Proverbs 5:18). "The wife of thy covenant" — with whom you made a solemn vow, "to violate which is a monstrous crime." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/malachi/2.htm)

---

## v. 15 — "Has not the LORD made them one, having a portion of the Spirit? And why one? Because He seeks godly offspring"

- **Extremely difficult Hebrew.** Ellicott devotes a long discussion, calling vv. 15–16 "two very difficult verses." His preferred rendering: "For did He not make [man and his wife, Genesis 2:24] one? and has he [the husband] any superiority of spirit [that he should divorce at will]? And what is this [pair which is become] one? [Answer.] It seeketh a godly seed." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **Keil's interpretation** (cited by Ellicott): The people object, "But what did the one [Abraham] do?" Answer: "He was seeking a seed of God" — i.e., Abraham dismissed Hagar in obedience to God's word (Genesis 21:12) to secure the promised seed through Isaac, not from carnal lust. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **Moore's interpretation** (cited by Ellicott): "Did not [God] make [us] one? Did He not separate us from other nations into an isolated unity? … Why [then did He choose] but one? He was seeking a seed of God [a nation which He should train up to be the repository of His covenant, the stock of His Messiah]." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: "Not any one has done so who has a remnant of the spirit (ruach)." No one acts as you have done who has in him any of that Divine life which God at first breathed into man — i.e., no man of conscience and virtue has ever thus divorced his wife. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/malachi/2.htm)
- **Guzik** reads it straightforwardly: God made husband and wife one, and one key reason is to establish a proper environment for raising godly offspring. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)
- **TGC (Reformed)**: "God's purpose for marriage also includes biological and spiritual fruitfulness. 'Godly offspring' continue the covenant community in which God normally nurtures a large portion of the next generation of His people." (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/malachi/)
- **Piper (DesiringGod)** renders it: "Has not the LORD made them one? In flesh and spirit they are his. And why one? Because he was seeking godly offspring." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/let-none-be-faithless-to-the-wife-of-his-youth)

> **Protestant differences on v. 15:** The Hebrew is notoriously difficult and translations diverge significantly. Most traditional Protestant commentators see it as referring to God making husband and wife "one" at creation (Genesis 2:24). Some (like Keil) see a reference to Abraham. The phrase "a remnant of the Spirit" / "portion of the Spirit" is debated — some see it as the human spirit, others as the Holy Spirit. Guzik (Pentecostal) reads it as about marital oneness; the TGC and Piper (Reformed) read it similarly, with emphasis on covenant offspring.

---

## v. 16 — "For I hate divorce … he who divorces his wife covers his garment with violence"

- **"I hate divorce" — the traditional reading.** Guzik states plainly: "There is no doubt that God hates divorce because it destroys what He loves — marriage." He gives three reasons: (1) it breaks a solemn vow, (2) it is harmful, (3) it illustrates apostasy and damnation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)
- **Biblical exceptions.** Guzik notes God allows divorce in two circumstances: sexual immorality (Matthew 19:1–9) and desertion by an unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:10–16). However, "misery, unhappiness, poverty, or incompatibilities are never given as grounds for divorce." Where there is danger or abuse, separation is in order per 1 Corinthians 7:10–11, but the couple must live in complete faithfulness to their vows. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)
- **TGC (Reformed)** notes the Hebrew at the beginning of v. 16 is "notoriously difficult." Many translations read "'I hate divorce' says the Lord," but TGC adds: "No matter how this phrase is translated, God's purpose is to rebuke husbands who wrongfully divorce their wives and to advocate for the mistreated women. Note that God hates the relational 'violence' of divorce, not all divorcees." TGC also notes that "Jesus confronted the misuse of Mosaic divorce legislation" and that "unfaithfulness may take other forms such as abuse or neglect that violate one's marriage vows (Exodus 21:10–11)." (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/malachi/)
- **Ellicott** reads it: "For [I] hate divorce [of the first wife], saith the God of Israel, and he [the divorcer of his first wife] covers his garment with injury." The word for "injury" (châmâs) is "especially used of ill-treatment of a wife" (Genesis 16:5). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **"Covers his garment with violence"** — Guzik explains the cultural background: part of the marriage ceremony involved the husband covering his wife with his garment as a symbol of protection. Now their garments were covered with violence instead. Because husband and wife are one, mistreating one's wife brings destruction on oneself (Ephesians 5:28). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)
- **Fortner (Baptist)** preached a sermon titled "HE HATETH PUTTING AWAY" and connected v. 16 to unconditional grace: "Because 'he hateth putting away' nothing can separate me from him!" — seeing in this a picture of God's faithfulness to His people. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fdc/malachi-2.html)

> **Protestant differences on v. 16:** All traditions affirm God's hatred of divorce and the sanctity of marriage. Differences emerge on the application of the exception clauses. Reformed and Baptist teachers (Guzik, Piper, TGC) hold to the traditional two grounds (adultery and desertion). Some stricter views (certain Reformed and fundamentalist Baptist) question remarriage after any divorce. The TGC commentary notably broadens "unfaithfulness" to potentially include "abuse or neglect that violate one's marriage vows" (citing Exodus 21:10–11), which represents a more recent Reformed discussion.

---

## v. 17 — "You have wearied the LORD with your words … 'All who do evil are good in the sight of the LORD' … 'Where is the God of justice?'"

- **The people's cynicism.** They looked at the world, saw the wicked prospering, and concluded either that God delights in evildoers or that there is no God of justice at all. Guzik: "The people of God in Malachi's day were depressed and discouraged because it seemed like the wicked prospered and had it better than the godly." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)
- **Ellicott** notes this verse opens a new section (extending into Malachi 3): the people's discontent and lack of faith because "the expected manifestation of God's glory did not take place immediately." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/2.htm)
- **Piper / Boice** (cited by Guzik): "God is offended when people accuse Him of injustice." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-2/)
- **Spurgeon** preached a sermon on Malachi 2:17 titled "Great Difference," addressing the distinction between the righteous and the wicked and God's ultimate justice. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/malachi_2_resources)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: The people "even posed the argument that God was pleased with what they were doing, else He would have already judged them. This verse serves as a transition to chapter three." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/malachi-2.html)

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Emphases Located

| Tradition | Source | Distinctive Emphasis |
|-----------|--------|---------------------|
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic** | EnduringWord (Guzik) | Practical application to personal holiness; "take heed to your spirit" emphasised as the key to changed feelings toward one's spouse; the Spirit's enabling |
| **Reformed** | TGC (Harmon), DesiringGod (Piper) | Covenant theology — the covenant with Levi points to Christ's priesthood; marriage as covenant reflecting Christ and the church; Levitical covenant as "life and peace" through conformity to God's law |
| **Baptist** | Garner-Howes, Fortner, Spurgeon | Literal-historical reading; emphasis on God's hatred of "putting away" linked to God's indestructible grace; the priests' failure as treachery from the pulpit |
| **Anglican (older)** | Ellicott, Pulpit Commentary | Detailed philological notes; careful textual criticism (e.g., "commandment" = decree); the "one father" as God, not Abraham |
| **Evangelical (broad)** | Precept Austin, Dr. Constable | Synthesis of multiple sources; emphasis on application for modern pastors — Wiersbe, MacArthur, Tozer, and Cole cited |

> **Catholic, Orthodox, modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org), and Methodist/Wesleyan/Lutheran tradition-specific pages** were searched but not found within the allowed source list for Malachi 2. These views are therefore omitted per the instruction to leave out what could not be found.
